full_text:
Sam Altman keeps insisting that AI progress is going better than the doomers predicted and that even superintelligence may not change the world as radically as people think. I react to his latest interview and explain why I think that calm, reassuring framing badly downplays the danger we’re actually in.

I go through the interview line by line: Sam’s “frame control”, his framing of AI as normal technology, his “pro-human” branding, the liberty-vs-safety pivot, and his victory lap on AI safety — all while his own AI just went rogue.

Don’t let them pull the Overton window backward.

What Is Frame Control?

Liron 00:03:12
The trick is what I call frame control. His MO — and it’s really not just him, it’s the other AI CEOs too. We actually had a Doom Debates episode, if you remember, a few months ago, where it was me and my guest, Harlan Stewart, from the Machine Intelligence Research Institute, and we were picking apart Dario Amodei’s essay from a few months ago. He swept that under the rug. Well, Sam Altman, he’s reading from the same playbook.

You’re gonna be hearing me repeat this concept a lot — frame control. I think it’s underappreciated because if you understand frame control, you can understand how a lot of human communication works that you’d otherwise not realize. You wouldn’t realize the game that’s being played around you.

So what do I mean? What is frame control? Frame control is the entire set of implicit background details, background implications, background assumptions that are being created in the listener’s mind when somebody’s talking, even if they’re not exactly the foreground of the words being said.

Think about improv. Think about a scene on stage. Somebody walks upstage, and he says, “Ooh, I’m getting pelted,” and he lifts his hands over his head, or he takes out an umbrella, opens the umbrella. Okay, well, the frame is they’re outside, and it’s raining. Even if he didn’t say, “I’m outside,” that’s already a good guess. He’s probably not getting rained on inside. And then he can say other things that imply a frame. He could be like, “Where are you guys?” Okay, well, that implies that there’s a bunch of guys, that there’s an expectation that the guys would be there.

This is very obvious when coming from the stage. This is the most intuitive thing in the world. But frame control becomes less intuitive when you realize that people live their lives broadcasting implicit frames. Normally, they don’t pay conscious attention to what implicit frame they’re broadcasting, but they are broadcasting it, and other people notice it. People like Sam Altman are pros at frame control, at communicating on that level.

Confidence is a type of frame control. If you walk outside and you’re strutting confidently and you’re acting like you don’t have a care in the world, you’re feeling good, well, you’re broadcasting a frame that your life is in good shape. Maybe something successful has happened. Maybe you just solved a problem. Something good is happening to you. That’s the frame that you’re broadcasting when you have the mannerisms of confidence.
